drills.q: Write the state vector of (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2) and give its Bloch coordinates.
drills.a: [1/sqrt(2), -1/sqrt(2)]; theta = pi/2 (equator), phi = pi. This is H|1>, the |- > state; measuring in the Z basis gives 50/50, after H it gives 1 deterministically.

drills.q: Compute X applied to alpha|0>+beta|1>, and Ry(pi/2)|0>.
How much RAM to hold a 40-qubit state vector in complex128?
Apply CNOT(control=0,target=1) to |10>. Then explain why CNOT alone on |+-> cannot create entanglement from every input.
drills.a: |10> -> |11> (control is 1, target flips). CNOT is a permutation and maps product states like |+-> to entangled states (it does create entanglement there); but on computational-basis inputs it only permutes bits and never entangles - entangling power depends on the input basis.

drills.q: Is (|00>+|01>+|10>+|11>)/2 entangled? Justify without full algebra.
drills.a: No: it factors as H|0> (x) H|0>, each qubit independently 50/50. Spread over all four basis strings is not entanglement; failure to factorise is.

drills.q: A teammate says their simulator 'uses the 2^70 amplitudes of its 70 qubits to compute in parallel'. Give the two-line rebuttal.
drills.a: 1) You cannot read those amplitudes: one measurement returns one 70-bit sample via the Born rule. 2) Without an interference schedule (an algorithm) plus error rates low enough to survive it, the amplitude space is unreachable structure, not usable memory.

drills.q: Given counts {'010': 498, '110': 502} from a 3-qubit circuit, which qubits are entangled and how would you verify?
drills.a: Qubit 1 is always 1 (deterministic); qubits 0 and 2 are perfectly anti... actually perfectly correlated with qubit1 fixed: they form a Bell-like pair across positions 0 and 2. Verify by computing reduced density matrices over {q0,q2} and checking purity Tr(rho^2) < 1, or run a SWAP test.

drills.q: Why does applying H twice return |0> while flipping a classical fair coin twice does not return heads?
drills.a: H acts on amplitudes: H(H|0>) = H((|0>+|1>)/sqrt2) = (|0>-|1>)/sqrt2 + ... sums to |0> exactly because amplitudes cancel/interfere. A coin mixer acts on probabilities, which are non-negative and cannot cancel.

drills.q: Your numpy simulator outputs probabilities that sum to 1 but disagree with Qiskit counts. First two things to check?
drills.a: 1) Endianness/qubit ordering: kron order vs Qiskit little-endian bitstrings. 2) Basis-change gates before measurement missing. Both are convention bugs, not linear-algebra bugs.

drills.q: Rank these claims for honesty: (A) '200 qubits explore 2^200 states', (B) 'our device prepares Bell pairs at 99% fidelity', (C) 'entanglement boosts our ML model accuracy'.
drills.a: (B) is falsifiable engineering language (state fidelity is measurable). (A) is dimension-counting marketing unless paired with an interference-based algorithm and readable output. (C) needs a baseline showing classical simulation of the same feature map loses - most such papers fail that control.

drills.q: What is the Schmidt rank of a two-qubit state, and how does it generalize the determinant test for entanglement?
drills.a: Reshape the state's coefficients into a matrix and take its SVD; Schmidt rank is the number of nonzero singular values. Rank 1 means separable (matching det(C)=0/rank(C)=1 for the 2x2 case); rank >1 means entangled, with the value quantifying how much. For 3+ qubits there is no single such scalar â€” e.g. GHZ and W states are both entangled but inequivalent under local operations.

drills.q: A recruiter-facing summary claims a quantum computer 'processes information exponentially faster because qubits explore all possibilities in parallel.' Give the precise one-sentence correction.
drills.a: Qubits don't freely 'explore in parallel' in a readable way â€” the exponential state space enables interference between computational paths during unitary evolution, and only specific algorithms with problem structure amenable to interference (Grover: quadratic, Shor: superpolynomial for period-finding) turn that into a proven, bounded, problem-specific speedup â€” never a generic exponential one.
